body.objective: Students will be able to write lyrics and melody.
body.iCan: I can write lyrics and melody.
successCriteria: I can write lyrics with a clear theme, imagery and rhyme
I can write a melody that fits the lyrics and chords
I can structure a song with verse, chorus and hook
body.hook: Most hit songs are built around a hook, a short catchy idea you can't get out of your head, often in the first 30 seconds. Writing a song starts with finding that hook and building everything else to support it.

study.title: Hook First
study.question: How do songwriters turn an idea into lyrics and melody?
study.passage:
Part 1, Title and theme (10 minutes): Brainstorm 10 possible song titles from your life (a place, a phrase someone says, a feeling). Pick one that could be the hook.
Part 2, Chorus lyrics (10 minutes): Write four lines that state the main idea. Put the title in the first or last line. Keep it simple and singable. Choose a rhyme scheme (AABB or ABAB).
Part 3, Verse lyrics (10 minutes): Write verse 1 with concrete imagery: show, don't tell. Instead of "I was sad," try "Your jacket's still on the hook by the door."
Part 4, Melody (15 minutes): Over a four-chord loop (for example C-G-Am-F), speak the chorus lyrics in rhythm, then sing them on pitches from the chords. Check prosody: stressed syllables should land on strong beats and higher or longer notes. Make the chorus melody higher or more energetic than the verse.
Part 5, Structure (5 minutes): Map the song: verse 1, chorus, verse 2, chorus, bridge, chorus. Record a voice memo of the draft.
study.source: Original songwriting workshop written for this lesson.
steps: Brainstorm titles and choose a hook
Write a chorus with the title
Write a verse with concrete imagery
Set lyrics to a melody with good prosody
Map the song structure and record a draft
discussion: Why put the title in the chorus?
How does concrete imagery make a verse stronger?
Where did prosody feel awkward and how did you fix it?
How is your chorus melody different from your verse?
study.product: Write and record a demo of an original song with at least one verse, a chorus with a hook and a clear structure map, then share it for feedback.

examples.title: Imagery
examples.answer: "Snow on the porch light, Mom's tea going cold"

examples.title: Prosody
examples.problem: The word "to-MOR-row" is sung with "to" on beat 1. What's wrong?
examples.answer: The unstressed syllable "to" falls on the strong beat; put "MOR" on the beat

examples.title: Chorus lift
examples.problem: How can a chorus melody stand out?
examples.answer: Use a higher range, longer notes or more rhythmic energy than the verse
examples.explore: What could the verse do instead?

practice.q: What does "show, don't tell" mean in lyrics?
practice.a: Use concrete details instead of stating feelings.

practice.q: How can you find a melody for lyrics?
practice.a: Speak them in rhythm, then sing on chord tones.

practice.q: Why should the chorus melody differ from the verse?
practice.a: Contrast makes the chorus lift and stand out.

practice.q: What job does a bridge do?
practice.a: Adds contrast or a new perspective before the final chorus.

practice.q: How can you fix bad prosody?
practice.a: Change the rhythm or the words so stresses land on strong beats.

practice.q: Why record a rough demo early?
practice.a: To hear and revise ideas before they're forgotten.

misconceptions: Thinking songs must rhyme perfectly every line
Writing vague lyrics with no concrete details
Thinking melody and lyrics are written separately and never adjusted

Label the rhyme scheme of four lines you wrote.
